old: BPC-157 is a synthetic pentadecapeptide (15 amino acids) originally discovered in human gastric juice, with remarkable stability in harsh environments like stomach acid.
Preclinical research demonstrates significant healing potential for tendons, ligaments, muscles, bones, and gastrointestinal tissues through multiple biological pathways.
The peptide operates through pleiotropic mechanisms, increasing pro-healing factors (VEGF, nitric oxide) while decreasing inflammatory markers (COX-2, IL-6, TNF-α).
Human clinical evidence remains limited, with only small pilot studies conducted; BPC-157 is currently designated for research use only and is not approved by regulatory agencies.

old.title: U.S. regulatory status — compounding policy (FDA status as of 29 October 2026)

entries.value: BPC-157 is not an FDA-approved drug and is not on the 503A Bulks List (21 CFR 216.23(a)). In 2026 two separate U.S. steps concerned BPC-157 and pharmacy compounding: a non-binding advisory committee vote in July and a draft interim enforcement-discretion policy that the HHS Office of the Secretary published for comment in October. Neither one approves BPC-157 or places it on the 503A Bulks List. BPC-157 was in FDA’s interim Category 2 from September 2023 until 22 April 2026. FDA’s categories list (updated 14 May 2026) does not place it in Category 1, 2 or 3.

Pharmacy Compounding Advisory Committee (23 July 2026). FDA’s Pharmacy Compounding Advisory Committee (PCAC) considered BPC-157 (free base) and BPC-157 acetate for the 503A Bulks List on 23 July 2026. In its briefing document, FDA proposed that neither form be included. FDA has not posted minutes or vote results on the meeting page, and this page gives no vote counts. The HHS policy’s Appendix B states that “Center for Drug Evaluation and Research (CDER) recommended against listing either form, and the Pharmacy Compounding Advisory Committee (PCAC) voted in favor of inclusion.” Advisory committee recommendations are non-binding.

Draft interim policy published for comment (Federal Register, 30 October 2026). The HHS Office of the Secretary published a notice of availability (FR Doc. 2026-22192; 91 FR 68526–68527; Docket No. HHS-OASH-2026-0496; RIN 0910-ZD94) for a draft “Enforcement Discretion Policy Regarding 503A Compounding Using Certain Peptide Bulk Drug Substances” on 30 October 2026. OIRA had concluded its review on 27 October 2026. The notice stated that written comments could be submitted “until 2 weeks after date of publication in the Federal Register”, and the regulations.gov docket lists the comment period as closed at 11:59 pm ET on 13 November 2026. As of 16 November 2026, no final version of the policy has been published and the docket lists no further notice. BPC-157 is one of six peptides in the policy’s Appendix A. The policy states that, until a peptide “is addressed in a final rule as being included or not included on the 503A bulks list,” HHS “does not intend to take action against a State licensed pharmacy, Federal facility, or licensed physician” compounding with it “when all of the following circumstances are present”.

Scope: the identity listed in Appendix B is BPC-157 acetate only, for “subcutaneous, intramuscular, oral, and topical dosage forms”, with the amino acid sequence Gly-Glu-Pro-Pro-Pro-Gly-Lys-Pro-Ala-Asp-Asp-Ala-Gly-Leu-Val. Other forms, including BPC-157 free base, are outside the listed identity. The compounded product may contain only a single active ingredient, so blends are outside the policy. For oral forms the compounder is expected to keep documentation of adequate oral bioavailability in humans. This describes the policy’s scope. It is not usage guidance.

Conditions (summary): the bulk substance must come from a facility registered under section 510 with a valid certificate of analysis (COA) whose test results meet the testing standard in Appendix B; the original manufacturer must be FDA-registered and CGMP-compliant, with its location on the certificate; compounders must report products compounded, serious adverse events and product quality issues to FDA and to the States, and serious adverse events and product quality issues to FDA’s MedWatch program; the label must state “This is a compounded drug product. Not for resale.”; the only co-packaged device may be an FDA 510(k)-cleared syringe; and section 503A’s insanitary-conditions and patient-specific prescription requirements still apply.

Not an approval: the notice states that “Compounded drugs are not FDA-approved, which means FDA does not review their safety, effectiveness, or quality before they are marketed.” The policy makes no safety or efficacy finding for BPC-157.

Not a Bulks List listing and not Category 1: BPC-157 is not on the 503A Bulks List (21 CFR 216.23(a)) and is not in any FDA interim category. The notice says FDA’s future rulemakings “may propose adding some or all of these peptides” to the list; no such proposed rule has been published.

Interim and non-binding: there is no calendar end date. The policy applies until a final rule addresses each peptide, HHS “may revisit” it “if, among other things, a safety signal or product quality issue arises”, and the notice says it “is not binding on HHS or the public.”

Research-use-only products: HHS describes the policy as meant to “discourage the continued, widespread use of certain research-use-only peptides supplied by foreign manufacturers that pose a safety risk to US patients.” Nothing in the policy treats research-use-only products as covered.

Other status lines are unchanged: on FDA’s "Certain Bulk Drug Substances for Use in Compounding that May Present Significant Safety Risks" page, BPC-157 is listed as nominated but withdrawn. BPC-157 remains on WADA’s S0 (non-approved substances) list.

old.title: Animal Safety Data

entries.value: One attractive feature of BPC-157 in research is its apparently favorable safety profile in animals. Toxicology studies have found no lethal dose even at extremely high amounts:
In rats, a single injection of 20 mg per kilogram (a massive dose for a peptide) caused no deaths or obvious toxic effects
In dogs, daily injections for a month at doses up to 1 mg/kg showed no significant adverse effects compared to control animals
Studies reported no changes in body weight, behavior, or organ health attributable to BPC-157

old.title: Theoretical Concerns

entries.value:
The most prominent theoretical concern is BPC-157's ability to promote growth factors and blood vessel formation. While beneficial for healing injuries, this raises a question: could BPC-157 unintentionally help existing cancer cells grow or spread? Cancerous tumors often exploit the same pathways (like FAK/paxillin and VEGF) to invade tissues and nourish themselves with blood supply.

This idea is currently theoretical – no study has shown BPC-157 causes cancer in animals or humans. In fact, one lab test showed BPC-157 inhibited growth of a particular cancer cell line in culture. Nonetheless, experts urge caution until more is known about long-term effects.

overview.old:
Dermorphin is a naturally occurring heptapeptide opioid first isolated from the skin of South American frogs of the genus Phyllomedusa. Sequence: H-Tyr-D-Ala-Phe-Gly-Tyr-Pro-Ser-NH₂. It is a highly potent, selective μ-opioid receptor (MOR) agonist in classic pharmacology assays. It is not FDA-approved as a medicine. Educational only—not medical advice; not a dosing guide.

Dermorphin is famous in peptide chemistry for containing a D-alanine at position 2—unusual among vertebrate peptides and essential for activity. Popular and grey-market interest sometimes frames it as a “natural super-opioid”; encyclopedia priority is accurate pharmacology literacy, clear preclinical vs clinical limits, and controlled-substance / diversion risk awareness. Marketplace powders are not approved analgesics.

old.title: FDA / compounding (FDA status as of 29 October 2026)

entries.value: Not FDA-approved, and not on the 503A Bulks List (21 CFR 216.23(a)). Epitalon here means the tetrapeptide Ala-Glu-Asp-Gly (AEDG). Epitalon was in FDA’s interim Category 2 from 29 September 2023 until 22 April 2026. FDA’s categories list (updated 14 May 2026) does not place it in Category 1, 2 or 3.

Pharmacy Compounding Advisory Committee (24 July 2026). FDA’s Pharmacy Compounding Advisory Committee (PCAC) considered Epitalon (free base) and Epitalon acetate for the 503A Bulks List on 24 July 2026. In its briefing document, FDA proposed that neither form be included. FDA has not posted minutes or vote results on the meeting page, and this page gives no vote counts. The HHS policy’s Appendix B states that “CDER recommended against listing either form, and the PCAC voted in favor of inclusion.” Advisory committee recommendations are non-binding.

Draft interim policy published for comment (Federal Register, 30 October 2026). The HHS Office of the Secretary published a notice of availability (FR Doc. 2026-22192; 91 FR 68526–68527; Docket No. HHS-OASH-2026-0496; RIN 0910-ZD94) for a draft “Enforcement Discretion Policy Regarding 503A Compounding Using Certain Peptide Bulk Drug Substances” on 30 October 2026. OIRA had concluded its review on 27 October 2026. The notice stated that written comments could be submitted “until 2 weeks after date of publication in the Federal Register”, and the regulations.gov docket lists the comment period as closed at 11:59 pm ET on 13 November 2026. As of 16 November 2026, no final version of the policy has been published and the docket lists no further notice. Epitalon is one of six peptides in the policy’s Appendix A. The policy states that, until a peptide “is addressed in a final rule as being included or not included on the 503A bulks list,” HHS “does not intend to take action against a State licensed pharmacy, Federal facility, or licensed physician” compounding with it “when all of the following circumstances are present”.

Scope: the identity listed in Appendix B is epitalon acetate (H-Ala-Glu-Asp-Gly-OH·CH3COOH), for subcutaneous or intramuscular injectable dosage forms “dispensed in intermittent courses”. The compounded product may contain only a single active ingredient. This describes the policy’s scope. It is not usage guidance.

Conditions (summary): the bulk substance must come from a facility registered under section 510 with a valid certificate of analysis (COA) whose test results meet the testing standard in Appendix B; the original manufacturer must be FDA-registered and CGMP-compliant, with its location on the certificate; compounders must report products compounded, serious adverse events and product quality issues to FDA and to the States, and serious adverse events and product quality issues to FDA’s MedWatch program; the label must state “This is a compounded drug product. Not for resale.”; the only co-packaged device may be an FDA 510(k)-cleared syringe; and section 503A’s insanitary-conditions and patient-specific prescription requirements still apply.

Not an approval: the notice states that “Compounded drugs are not FDA-approved, which means FDA does not review their safety, effectiveness, or quality before they are marketed.” The policy makes no safety or efficacy finding for Epitalon.

Not a Bulks List listing and not Category 1: Epitalon is not on the 503A Bulks List (21 CFR 216.23(a)) and is not in any FDA interim category. The notice says FDA’s future rulemakings “may propose adding some or all of these peptides” to the list; no such proposed rule has been published.

Interim and non-binding: there is no calendar end date. The policy applies until a final rule addresses each peptide, HHS “may revisit” it “if, among other things, a safety signal or product quality issue arises”, and the notice says it “is not binding on HHS or the public.”

Research-use-only products: HHS describes the policy as meant to “discourage the continued, widespread use of certain research-use-only peptides supplied by foreign manufacturers that pose a safety risk to US patients.” Nothing in the policy treats research-use-only products as covered.

entries.value: Not an FDA-approved drug, and not on the 503A Bulks List (21 CFR 216.23(a)). KPV here means the tripeptide Lys-Pro-Val (CAS 67727-97-3). KPV was in FDA’s interim Category 2 from September 2023 until 22 April 2026. FDA’s categories list (updated 14 May 2026) does not place it in Category 1, 2 or 3.

Pharmacy Compounding Advisory Committee (23 July 2026). FDA’s Pharmacy Compounding Advisory Committee (PCAC) considered KPV (free base) and KPV acetate for the 503A Bulks List on 23 July 2026. In its briefing document, FDA proposed that neither form be included. FDA has not posted minutes or vote results on the meeting page, and this page gives no vote counts. The HHS policy’s Appendix B states that “CDER recommended against listing either form, and the PCAC voted in favor of inclusion.” Advisory committee recommendations are non-binding.

Draft interim policy published for comment (Federal Register, 30 October 2026). The HHS Office of the Secretary published a notice of availability (FR Doc. 2026-22192; 91 FR 68526–68527; Docket No. HHS-OASH-2026-0496; RIN 0910-ZD94) for a draft “Enforcement Discretion Policy Regarding 503A Compounding Using Certain Peptide Bulk Drug Substances” on 30 October 2026. OIRA had concluded its review on 27 October 2026. The notice stated that written comments could be submitted “until 2 weeks after date of publication in the Federal Register”, and the regulations.gov docket lists the comment period as closed at 11:59 pm ET on 13 November 2026. As of 16 November 2026, no final version of the policy has been published and the docket lists no further notice. KPV is one of six peptides in the policy’s Appendix A. The policy states that, until a peptide “is addressed in a final rule as being included or not included on the 503A bulks list,” HHS “does not intend to take action against a State licensed pharmacy, Federal facility, or licensed physician” compounding with it “when all of the following circumstances are present”.

Scope: the identity listed in Appendix B is KPV acetate only, for “topical and oral dosage forms”. No injectable route is listed. For oral forms the compounder is expected to keep documentation of adequate oral bioavailability in humans. The compounded product may contain only a single active ingredient, so blends such as KLOW are outside the policy. This describes the policy’s scope. It is not usage guidance.

Conditions (summary): the bulk substance must come from a facility registered under section 510 with a valid certificate of analysis (COA) whose test results meet the testing standard in Appendix B; the original manufacturer must be FDA-registered and CGMP-compliant, with its location on the certificate; compounders must report products compounded, serious adverse events and product quality issues to FDA and to the States, and serious adverse events and product quality issues to FDA’s MedWatch program; the label must state “This is a compounded drug product. Not for resale.”; the only co-packaged device may be an FDA 510(k)-cleared syringe; and section 503A’s insanitary-conditions and patient-specific prescription requirements still apply.

Not an approval: the notice states that “Compounded drugs are not FDA-approved, which means FDA does not review their safety, effectiveness, or quality before they are marketed.” The policy makes no safety or efficacy finding for KPV.

Not a Bulks List listing and not Category 1: KPV is not on the 503A Bulks List (21 CFR 216.23(a)) and is not in any FDA interim category. The notice says FDA’s future rulemakings “may propose adding some or all of these peptides” to the list; no such proposed rule has been published.

Interim and non-binding: there is no calendar end date. The policy applies until a final rule addresses each peptide, HHS “may revisit” it “if, among other things, a safety signal or product quality issue arises”, and the notice says it “is not binding on HHS or the public.”

Research-use-only products: HHS describes the policy as meant to “discourage the continued, widespread use of certain research-use-only peptides supplied by foreign manufacturers that pose a safety risk to US patients.” Nothing in the policy treats research-use-only products as covered.

overview.old:
Retatrutide (LY3437943) is an investigational triple hormone receptor agonist (GIP, GLP-1, and glucagon receptors) studied as a once-weekly injectable in clinical trials. It is not FDA-approved and is not a marketed medicine. PeptideMap covers it as research news + RUO vendor comparison — not therapy guidance.

Detailed Phase 3 results from TRIUMPH-2 (adults with type 2 diabetes and obesity or overweight; n=1,152; 80 weeks) were presented at EASD 2026 and published in The Lancet (29 Sep 2026). Under Lilly’s efficacy estimand, mean body-weight change at week 80 was −12.7% (4 mg arm), −19.1% (9 mg arm), and −20.8% (12 mg arm) versus −4.0% with placebo; A1C fell about 1.4–1.6 percentage points versus −0.2 with placebo. The Lancet abstract also reports treatment-regimen mean percent weight change of −11.9%, −16.8%, and −18.8% versus −5.1% placebo. GI adverse events were the most common reported events in the trial; Lilly has said it plans to file a U.S. application no later than Q1 2027, and FDA concluded on 2 October 2026 that the application would need to go under section 505 of the Federal Food, Drug, and Cosmetic Act (filing plan ≠ approval).

Also known in research-vendor catalogs as GLP3-R — PeptideMap lists Retatrutide as the primary name. Grey-market / RUO listings are not clinical trial supply.

Timeline literacy (as of 22 Oct 2026): Retatrutide (LY3437943) is still an investigational triple agonist. It is not FDA-approved and is not a sponsor-marketed medicine. Lilly’s 23 July 2026 topline on TRIUMPH-2 and TRIUMPH-3 stated that the company is completing the Chemistry, Manufacturing, and Controls (CMC) package required for a Biologics License Application and plans to submit in Q1 2027 for U.S. review — a company filing plan, not FDA acceptance and not approval. On 2 October 2026, in a decision on remand, FDA concluded that retatrutide is not a biological product and that an application would need to be submitted under section 505 of the Federal Food, Drug, and Cosmetic Act; Lilly’s related Seventh Circuit appeal (No. 26-1301) had no ruling as of 22 October 2026. Grey-market / RUO catalog vials are not clinical-trial supply and are not expanded-access supply.

old.title: Biologic vs drug classification — FDA decision on remand (2 Oct 2026); Seventh Circuit appeal pending

entries.value: In January 2024, Lilly asked FDA to regulate retatrutide as a biological product under a Biologics License Application (BLA). FDA responded on 18 March 2024 that retatrutide is a drug, not a biological product. Lilly sued in the U.S. District Court for the Southern District of Indiana (No. 1:24-cv-01503), which sent issues about whether retatrutide is “analogous” to a protein back to FDA. On 2 October 2026, deciding those issues on remand, FDA’s Center for Drug Evaluation and Research concluded that “retatrutide is not an analogous product to a protein and is therefore not a biological product. Accordingly, an application for retatrutide would need to be submitted under section 505 of the Federal Food, Drug, and Cosmetic Act.” A redacted copy of the decision was filed in the Seventh Circuit on 8 October 2026 (No. 26-1301, Dkt. 46-2).

Lilly’s appeal in the U.S. Court of Appeals for the Seventh Circuit, Eli Lilly and Company v. Robert F. Kennedy, Jr., No. 26-1301, is from the district court’s judgment. The court heard oral argument on 24 September 2026 and ordered supplemental memoranda on appellate jurisdiction, which both sides filed on 8 October 2026 (Dkt. 45–47). In a footnote, Lilly’s memorandum says FDA’s new decision is “beyond the scope of this appeal” (Dkt. 47, n.3). As of 22 October 2026, no ruling appeared on the docket.

Educational takeaway only: under FDA’s 2 October 2026 decision, an application for retatrutide would be a section 505 drug application. Neither that classification decision nor the pending appeal is an approval decision, and an argument or a pending appeal is not a ruling.

old.title: Access before approval — trials vs expanded access vs grey-market

entries.value: Before any approval, legitimate pathways discussed in primary manufacturer/FDA-process materials are clinical trials and, in limited circumstances, expanded access (sometimes called compassionate use) coordinated with a treating physician and applicable FDA IND / IRB requirements.

Lilly Medical states that retatrutide is not currently FDA-approved; that Lilly is supporting single-patient expanded-access requests for individuals who meet eligibility criteria when they cannot join a trial and have exhausted available options; that availability depends on geography, supply, and case-by-case assessment; and that requests are physician-initiated. High-level eligibility themes on Lilly Medical include refractory obesity (BMI ≥35 despite highest tolerated approved chronic weight-management therapy), at least two serious or life-threatening obesity-related complications under standard care, and inability to join an ongoing retatrutide (or comparable) trial. This page does not turn those criteria into an application guide or medical advice.
Grey-market / RUO vials sold online are not clinical-trial supply and are not expanded access. Catalog adjacency is not a manufacturer program.

Lilly has said it plans to file a U.S. application no later than Q1 2027, and FDA concluded on 2 October 2026 that such an application would need to be submitted under section 505 (the drug pathway); a filing plan is not marketing authorization. old.title: U.S. compounding policy (FDA status as of 29 October 2026)

entries.value: TB-500 on this page means the synthetic fragment Ac-LKKTETQ (Ac-Leu-Lys-Lys-Thr-Glu-Thr-Gln-OH), not full-length thymosin beta-4. TB-500 is not an FDA-approved drug and is not on the 503A Bulks List (21 CFR 216.23(a)). TB-500 was in FDA’s interim Category 2 from 29 September 2023 until 22 April 2026. FDA’s categories list (updated 14 May 2026) does not place it in Category 1, 2 or 3.

Pharmacy Compounding Advisory Committee (23 July 2026). FDA’s Pharmacy Compounding Advisory Committee (PCAC) considered TB-500 (free base) and TB-500 acetate for the 503A Bulks List on 23 July 2026. In its briefing document, FDA proposed that neither form be included. FDA has not posted minutes or vote results on the meeting page, and this page gives no vote counts. The HHS policy’s Appendix B states that “CDER recommended against listing either form, and the PCAC voted in favor of both forms.” Advisory committee recommendations are non-binding.

Draft interim policy published for comment (Federal Register, 30 October 2026). The HHS Office of the Secretary published a notice of availability (FR Doc. 2026-22192; 91 FR 68526–68527; Docket No. HHS-OASH-2026-0496; RIN 0910-ZD94) for a draft “Enforcement Discretion Policy Regarding 503A Compounding Using Certain Peptide Bulk Drug Substances” on 30 October 2026. OIRA had concluded its review on 27 October 2026. The notice stated that written comments could be submitted “until 2 weeks after date of publication in the Federal Register”, and the regulations.gov docket lists the comment period as closed at 11:59 pm ET on 13 November 2026. As of 16 November 2026, no final version of the policy has been published and the docket lists no further notice. TB-500 is one of six peptides in the policy’s Appendix A. The policy states that, until a peptide “is addressed in a final rule as being included or not included on the 503A bulks list,” HHS “does not intend to take action against a State licensed pharmacy, Federal facility, or licensed physician” compounding with it “when all of the following circumstances are present”.

Scope: the identity listed in Appendix B is TB-500 acetate (Ac-Leu-Lys-Lys-Thr-Glu-Thr-Gln-OH·CH3COOH), for “subcutaneous or intramuscular injectable dosage forms” only. Full-length thymosin beta-4 is not the listed identity. The compounded product may contain only a single active ingredient, so blends such as BPC-157 with TB-500 are outside the policy. This describes the policy’s scope. It is not usage guidance.

Conditions (summary): the bulk substance must come from a facility registered under section 510 with a valid certificate of analysis (COA) whose test results meet the testing standard in Appendix B; the original manufacturer must be FDA-registered and CGMP-compliant, with its location on the certificate; compounders must report products compounded, serious adverse events and product quality issues to FDA and to the States, and serious adverse events and product quality issues to FDA’s MedWatch program; the label must state “This is a compounded drug product. Not for resale.”; the only co-packaged device may be an FDA 510(k)-cleared syringe; and section 503A’s insanitary-conditions and patient-specific prescription requirements still apply.

Not an approval: the notice states that “Compounded drugs are not FDA-approved, which means FDA does not review their safety, effectiveness, or quality before they are marketed.” The policy makes no safety or efficacy finding for TB-500.

Not a Bulks List listing and not Category 1: TB-500 is not on the 503A Bulks List (21 CFR 216.23(a)) and is not in any FDA interim category. The notice says FDA’s future rulemakings “may propose adding some or all of these peptides” to the list; no such proposed rule has been published.

Interim and non-binding: there is no calendar end date. The policy applies until a final rule addresses each peptide, HHS “may revisit” it “if, among other things, a safety signal or product quality issue arises”, and the notice says it “is not binding on HHS or the public.”

Research-use-only products: HHS describes the policy as meant to “discourage the continued, widespread use of certain research-use-only peptides supplied by foreign manufacturers that pose a safety risk to US patients.” Nothing in the policy treats research-use-only products as covered.

entries.value: Tirzepatide is FDA-approved as branded medicines from Eli Lilly. Mounjaro is approved for type 2 diabetes (May 2022) and to lower the risk of major cardiovascular events in adults with type 2 diabetes at high cardiovascular risk (August 2026). Zepbound is approved for chronic weight management (November 2023) and for moderate to severe obstructive sleep apnea in adults with obesity (December 2024). In December 2024 the FDA declared the tirzepatide shortage resolved, which began the end of the temporary allowance for compounding pharmacies to make copies.
